items.q: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after spending 25,000 pounds on three luxury cars, claiming he has been chosen by the government to run the national economy. Over the past six days, he has slept only two hours per night, speaks in an unstoppable torrent of ideas, and behaves impulsively. According to NICE guideline CG185, what is the recommended first-line treatment for acute mania?
o: Oral atypical antipsychotic (e.g. olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, or haloperidol)
Oral selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (e.g. sertraline)
items.exp: NICE guideline CG185 recommends offering an oral atypical antipsychotic (haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, or risperidone) as first-line medical treatment for patients presenting with an acute manic episode.
r: Correct: An oral atypical antipsychotic is the recommended first-line treatment for acute mania.
SSRIs are strictly contraindicated in acute mania as they exacerbate manic excitement and psychosis.
Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat core manic psychosis or mood elevation.
ECT is reserved for severe, life-threatening, treatment-resistant mania or severe catatonia, not initial first-line.
items.kp: First-line medical treatment for acute mania is an oral atypical antipsychotic (e.g. olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone).
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Oral atypical antipsychotics are first-line for acute mania per NICE CG185.

others.D: ECT is reserved for refractory mania.

x.pearl: If the patient is already taking an antidepressant, it must be stopped immediately upon presentation with mania.
x.clues: Grandiosity, reckless spending, decreased sleep, pressured speech, acute mania first-line treatment.
x.ddx: Schizoaffective disorder, drug-induced psychosis (cocaine/amphetamines), delirium, hyperthyroidism.
x.mech: Dopamine D2 and 5-HT2A receptor antagonism rapidly attenuates hyperdopaminergic neurotransmission in the mesolimbic pathway.
x.lo: Select the first-line pharmacological treatment for an acute manic episode.
x.rev: Oral atypical antipsychotics are first-line for acute mania per NICE CG185.

items.q: A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has recovered from his second manic episode and is being discharged from the inpatient psychiatric unit. Which medication is the established first-line long-term maintenance mood stabilizer with robust evidence for reducing both manic relapses and suicide mortality?
items.exp: NICE guideline CG185 establishes lithium carbonate as the primary first-line long-term maintenance therapy for bipolar disorder. Lithium is uniquely proven to prevent both manic and depressive relapses and substantially reduces completed suicide mortality.
r: Correct: Lithium is the first-line long-term mood stabilizer that uniquely reduces suicide mortality.
Fluoxetine monotherapy destabilizes mood and can trigger manic relapses in bipolar I.
Venlafaxine carries a high risk of manic switching and is not a mood stabilizer.
Lamotrigine is effective predominantly for depressive prevention, but lacks efficacy in preventing manic relapses.
items.kp: Lithium carbonate is the first-line maintenance mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder and uniquely reduces suicide risk.
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Lithium carbonate is first-line maintenance in bipolar disorder and lowers suicide risk.
x.pearl: Lithium is one of the very few psychiatric medications with proven independent anti-suicide properties beyond general symptom control.
x.clues: Bipolar I maintenance, prevents manic relapses, reduces suicide mortality.
x.mech: Inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) and inositol monophosphatase (IMPase), promoting neuroprotective cellular signaling.
x.lo: Identify lithium as the first-line maintenance therapy for bipolar disorder.
x.rev: Lithium carbonate is the first-line maintenance mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder.

items.q: A 36-year-old woman stabilized on lithium carbonate attends the psychiatric outpatient clinic for routine monitoring. What is the standard target 12-hour post-dose serum trough concentration for maintenance therapy in bipolar disorder?
items.exp: NICE guideline CG185 specifies that for long-term maintenance therapy in bipolar disorder, serum lithium concentrations should be maintained within a target range of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L. For patients who have relapsed or have subthreshold symptoms, the range may be adjusted to 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L.
r: Correct: Target 12-hour trough lithium range for maintenance is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
0.2 to 0.4 mmol/L is subtherapeutic and fails to prevent relapses.
1.2 to 1.6 mmol/L borders on toxicity and is too high for routine maintenance.
2.0 to 2.5 mmol/L represents severe life-threatening lithium toxicity.
items.kp: Target 12-hour serum lithium trough concentration for bipolar maintenance is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Target 12-hour trough lithium concentration for maintenance is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.
x.pearl: Blood samples for serum lithium must be drawn precisely 12 hours after the preceding evening dose to ensure accurate trough assessment.
x.clues: Lithium maintenance, target 12-hour post-dose trough serum level.
x.ddx: Acute treatment range (0.8-1.0 mmol/L), toxic threshold (>1.5 mmol/L).
x.mech: Narrow therapeutic index requires close monitoring to balance GSK-3 inhibition against renal and neurological toxicity.
x.lo: State the therapeutic target range for serum lithium maintenance therapy.
x.rev: Target 12-hour serum lithium trough level for bipolar maintenance is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.

next.text: Review therapeutic drug monitoring of lithium.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman on long-term lithium therapy for bipolar disorder presents to the emergency department with coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech (dysarthria), vomiting, and dehydration. Her serum lithium concentration is 2.2 mmol/L. She reports recently starting an over-the-counter medication for knee osteoarthritis. Which drug class commonly precipitates lithium toxicity by impairing renal clearance?
items.exp: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac) inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, reducing renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate, which decreases lithium excretion and dramatically raises serum lithium concentrations, precipitating severe toxicity. Thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs have similar toxic interactions.
r: Correct: NSAIDs impair renal lithium clearance and precipitate severe toxicity.
Paracetamol has no significant effect on renal prostaglandin synthesis or lithium excretion.
Topical capsaicin is non-systemic and does not interact with lithium.
Glucosamine has no known pharmacokinetic interaction with lithium.
items.kp: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazide diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium and precipitate toxicity.
items.source: British National Formulary / NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder

x.key: NSAIDs impair renal lithium clearance, precipitating life-threatening toxicity.

others.B: Paracetamol does not alter lithium clearance.

x.pearl: The mnemonic 'DAAN' summarizes drugs that elevate lithium levels: Diuretics (thiazides), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and NSAIDs.
x.clues: Lithium toxicity (ataxia, coarse tremor, vomiting), serum level 2.2 mmol/L, OTC arthritis drug.
x.ddx: Dehydration, intercurrent gastroenteritis, overdose, renal failure.
x.mech: Inhibition of renal cyclooxygenases reduces renal medullary blood flow and enhances proximal tubular lithium reabsorption.
x.lo: Identify dangerous drug interactions that precipitate lithium toxicity.
x.rev: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazides reduce renal lithium excretion and cause toxicity.

next.text: Review lithium drug interactions in the BNF.

items.q: A 25-year-old man is being prepared for initiation of lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder. In accordance with NICE guideline CG185, which baseline investigations must be documented before starting lithium therapy?
o: Renal function (urea, creatinine, eGFR), electrolytes, thyroid function (TSH), calcium, and ECG
Liver function tests and coagulation screen only
Full blood count, blood film, and serum ferritin only
items.exp: NICE guideline CG185 requires baseline assessment of renal function (urea, creatinine, eGFR), serum electrolytes, thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4), serum calcium, weight/BMI, and an ECG (especially in patients with cardiovascular risk factors) prior to initiating lithium therapy.
r: Correct: Renal, thyroid, calcium, electrolytes, and ECG are essential baseline tests before starting lithium.
Liver function and coagulation tests do not address the major target organs of lithium toxicity.
FBC and ferritin are not the primary baseline monitoring parameters for lithium.
Lumbar puncture and EEG are invasive and unindicated for baseline lithium monitoring.
items.kp: Mandatory baseline tests before starting lithium include renal function, electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, and an ECG.
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Baseline renal function, thyroid function, electrolytes, calcium, and ECG are mandatory before lithium.
x.pearl: Renal and thyroid function must be monitored at least every 6 months while the patient remains on lithium therapy.
x.clues: Before starting lithium, mandatory baseline investigations.
x.ddx: Baseline tests for valproate (LFTs, FBC), baseline tests for clozapine (FBC, absolute neutrophil count).
x.mech: Lithium is cleared exclusively by the kidneys and can induce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular interstitial nephritis, and hypothyroidism.
x.lo: List the essential baseline investigations required prior to initiating lithium therapy.
x.rev: Renal function, thyroid function, electrolytes, calcium, and ECG are required before starting lithium.

next.text: Review NICE CG185 lithium monitoring schedule.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is being considered for maintenance therapy. Her psychiatrist notes that sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in girls and women of childbearing potential unless conditions of a Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met. What are the major risks of in utero sodium valproate exposure?
o: High rate of major congenital malformations (10%, including neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental delay (30-40%)
Isolated neonatal hypoglycaemia without physical malformations
Transient maternal alopecia without fetal effect
items.exp: Sodium valproate is profoundly teratogenic. In utero exposure causes a 10% rate of major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, craniofacial defects, cardiac malformations, hypospadias) and a 30-40% incidence of long-term neurodevelopmental disorders, cognitive impairment, and autism spectrum disorders. MHRA and NICE strictly restrict its use in women of childbearing potential.
r: Correct: Valproate causes 10% major malformations (neural tube defects) and 30-40% neurodevelopmental disability.
Valproate risks are far more severe than isolated neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Valproate causes severe permanent structural and developmental damage, not mild jitteriness.
Fetal risks are devastating and permanent, not limited to maternal alopecia.
items.kp: Sodium valproate in pregnancy causes a 10% rate of major malformations and a 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental disorders.
items.source: MHRA Drug Safety Update / NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder

x.key: Valproate causes a 10% rate of major malformations and 30-40% neurodevelopmental disorders.

others.C: Severe permanent defects, not mild jitteriness.

x.pearl: The MHRA Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form must be signed annually if valproate is prescribed to any female of childbearing potential.
x.clues: Woman of childbearing potential, bipolar, valproate contraindication rationale.
x.mech: Valproate acts as a histone deacetylase inhibitor, disrupting embryonic neural tube closure and cortical neuronal migration.
x.lo: Explain the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of sodium valproate in pregnancy.
x.rev: Valproate carries a 10% malformation risk and 30-40% neurodevelopmental disorder risk in exposed offspring.

next.text: Review MHRA valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

items.q: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder stabilized on lithium carbonate discovers she is 7 weeks pregnant. What specific congenital cardiovascular malformation is classically associated with first-trimester in utero lithium exposure?
o: Ebstein anomaly (downward displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets)
items.exp: First-trimester in utero lithium exposure is classically associated with Ebstein anomaly, a congenital cardiac defect characterized by apical (downward) displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle, leading to 'atrialization' of the right ventricle and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
r: Correct: Ebstein anomaly (tricuspid valve apical displacement) is classically linked to first-trimester lithium exposure.
Tetralogy of Fallot is associated with 22q11 deletion and maternal diabetes, not lithium.
Coarctation of the aorta is famously linked to Turner syndrome.
Transposition of the great arteries is linked to pre-gestational maternal diabetes mellitus.
items.kp: First-trimester lithium exposure is classically associated with Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve.
items.source: NICE guideline CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health

x.key: First-trimester lithium exposure is linked to Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve.

others.C: Coarctation is linked to Turner syndrome.
others.D: Transposition is linked to maternal diabetes.

x.pearl: Although the relative risk of Ebstein anomaly is elevated roughly tenfold by lithium, the absolute risk remains modest (approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 2,000 exposed pregnancies).
x.clues: Pregnant woman on lithium in first trimester, specific congenital heart defect.
x.ddx: Valproate (neural tube defects), carbamazepine (spina bifida, craniofacial defects).
x.mech: Disruption of embryonic cardiac looping and endocardial cushion differentiation mediated by GSK-3 inhibition.
x.lo: Identify Ebstein anomaly as the specific cardiac defect associated with lithium exposure in pregnancy.
x.rev: First-trimester lithium exposure carries a specific risk of Ebstein anomaly.

next.text: Review teratogenic cardiac defects in psychiatry.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman with a documented history of bipolar I disorder presents with a severe depressive episode characterized by profound anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, and nihilistic thoughts. Why does NICE guideline CG185 warn against prescribing antidepressant monotherapy (such as citalopram or venlafaxine alone) for bipolar depression?
o: High risk of precipitating a manic switch or rapid mood cycling
Antidepressants are 100% ineffective in all forms of depression
Antidepressants induce irreversible Parkinsonism in bipolar patients
Antidepressants invariably cause hypertensive crisis when given to bipolar patients
items.exp: NICE guideline CG185 strongly advises against antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder because unmitigated antidepressant exposure carries a high risk of inducing a pharmacological 'manic switch' (precipitating hypomania or mania) or triggering destabilizing rapid cycling. Bipolar depression is managed with medications such as quetiapine, olanzapine (plus fluoxetine), or lurasidone.
r: Correct: Antidepressant monotherapy carries a dangerous risk of triggering a manic switch or rapid cycling.
Antidepressants are effective for unipolar depression, but dangerous when given alone in bipolar disorder.
Antidepressants do not cause irreversible Parkinsonism.
Antidepressants do not cause hypertensive crises unless non-selective MAOIs interact with tyramine.
items.kp: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression is contraindicated due to the risk of triggering a manic switch or rapid cycling.
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Antidepressant monotherapy risks triggering a manic switch or rapid cycling in bipolar disorder.

others.D: They do not cause hypertensive crises.

x.pearl: If an antidepressant is used for bipolar depression, it must ALWAYS be co-prescribed with an antimanic mood stabilizer (such as lithium or an atypical antipsychotic).
x.clues: Bipolar depression, warning against antidepressant monotherapy.
x.ddx: Unipolar major depression, dysthymia, schizoaffective disorder.
x.mech: Monoaminergic upregulation in sensitized mesolimbic circuits triggers sudden polarity reversal from depression to manic excitement.
x.lo: Explain why antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar depression.
x.rev: Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar disorder due to the risk of inducing a manic switch.

items.q: A clinician is evaluating a 29-year-old woman who has had 5 days of elevated mood, increased energy, and reduced need for sleep. She has been very productive at her office, and colleagues note she is more sociable and talkative than usual. There are no psychotic features, and her social and occupational functioning is preserved without disruption. What distinguishes this hypomanic episode from full mania?
o: Absence of severe functional disruption, absence of psychotic symptoms, and no requirement for hospitalisation
items.exp: In accordance with ICD-11 and DSM-5, hypomania is characterized by elevated or irritable mood lasting at least 4 consecutive days that is clearly different from usual, but WITHOUT severe disruption of social or occupational functioning, WITHOUT psychotic features, and NEVER requiring hospital admission. The presence of ANY psychotic symptom or the need for hospitalisation automatically defines full mania.
r: Correct: Hypomania lacks severe functional breakdown, psychotic features, and hospitalisation.
The presence of psychotic symptoms automatically converts the diagnosis to mania.
Duration of 3 weeks does not define hypomania; mania can last any duration >=7 days.
Catatonic posturing indicates severe catatonic mania or affective psychosis.
items.kp: Hypomania differs from mania by the absence of psychotic symptoms, no severe functional disruption, and no hospitalisation.

x.key: Hypomania lacks severe functional impairment, psychotic features, and hospitalisation.
x.pearl: Patients often enjoy hypomania and do not seek help during these phases; diagnosis relies on collateral history from family or partners.
x.clues: 5 days elevated mood, increased work productivity, no severe disruption, no psychosis.
x.ddx: Mania, cyclothymia, ADHD, hyperthyroidism, stimulant abuse.
x.mech: Moderate dopaminergic and noradrenergic hyperactivity sufficient to enhance vigilance without disorganized thought disruption.
x.lo: Differentiate hypomania from mania based on functional impairment, psychosis, and hospitalisation.
x.rev: Hypomania lacks severe functional disruption, psychotic symptoms, and need for hospitalisation.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman taking lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder for the past 12 years attends her routine annual check-up. She complains of progressive cold intolerance, dry skin, fatigue, and modest weight gain. Laboratory results show: TSH 14.5 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0), free T4 7.2 pmol/L (normal 9.0-25.0). Serum lithium is 0.72 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis and recommended clinical management?
o: Lithium-induced primary hypothyroidism; initiate oral levothyroxine replacement and continue lithium if clinically indicated
Immediate discontinuation of lithium with no endocrine replacement
Myxoedema coma; immediate intravenous liothyronine and hydrocortisone in ICU
items.exp: Lithium concentrates in the thyroid gland and inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and release, causing hypothyroidism in up to 20% of long-term users. The recommended management is to continue lithium (if effective for mood stabilization) and initiate oral levothyroxine replacement, titrating to normalize TSH.
r: Correct: Initiate levothyroxine replacement while continuing lithium if clinically indicated.
Discontinuing lithium abruptly triggers severe bipolar relapse and does not rapidly reverse established hypothyroidism.
Haemodialysis is indicated for life-threatening lithium toxicity (>4.0 mmol/L or severe neurological signs), not a therapeutic level of 0.72.
The patient is ambulatory with mild symptoms, not in myxoedema coma.
items.kp: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is treated by initiating levothyroxine replacement while continuing lithium therapy.
items.source: NICE guideline CG185: Bipolar disorder: assessment and management

x.key: Treat lithium-induced hypothyroidism with levothyroxine while maintaining lithium.

others.D: Patient is ambulatory, not in coma.

x.pearl: Hypothyroidism is not a contraindication to continuing lithium; simply co-prescribe levothyroxine to maintain euthyroid status.
x.clues: Long-term lithium user, cold intolerance, fatigue, high TSH, low T4, therapeutic lithium level.
x.ddx: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, central hypothyroidism.
x.mech: Lithium interferes with thyroidal iodine uptake, iodotyrosine coupling, and colloid droplet resorption, blocking T3/T4 secretion.
x.lo: Manage lithium-induced hypothyroidism appropriately with levothyroxine replacement.
x.rev: Manage lithium-induced hypothyroidism with levothyroxine while continuing lithium.
